structured.name: Sierra Leone
structured.naturalResources: diamonds, titanium ore, bauxite, iron ore, gold, chromite
structured._source: wikidata (CC0); landBorders + naturalResources from CIA World Factbook (public domain)

prose.hook: Tucked between Guinea and Liberia on West Africa's Atlantic coast, this is a land of mangrove swamps, wooded hills, an upland plateau, and mountains further east. Its coast is one of the wettest stretches of coastal West Africa, with rainfall reaching 495 cm (195 in) a year. Beneath the ground lies a wealth of diamonds, titanium ore, bauxite, iron ore, gold, and chromite, resources that shape much of what the country exports today.
prose.physicalGeography: The landscape moves inland in bands: a coastal belt of mangrove swamps gives way to wooded hill country, then an upland plateau, with mountains rising in the east. The country sits on West Africa's Atlantic coast, bordered by Guinea and Liberia.
prose.climate: The climate is tropical, hot and humid, with a rainy season running from May to December and a dry season from December to April. Between December and February, dry, sand-laden harmattan winds blow in from the Sahara, bringing sandstorms and dust storms.
prose.economy: This is a low-income economy built largely on subsistence agriculture, even though the country is rich in natural resources. Key iron and diamond mining activities have been suspended, and recovery from the 1990s civil war has been slow, compounded by systemic corruption, high-risk debt, and high youth unemployment. Industries include diamond mining, iron ore, rutile, and bauxite extraction, along with small-scale manufacturing of beverages, textiles, and footwear, and recent exports include iron ore, titanium ore, diamonds, aluminum ore, and cocoa beans.
prose.peopleAndCulture: English is the official language but in regular use only among a literate minority, while Mende dominates in the south and Temne in the north. Krio, an English-based Creole spoken by descendants of freed Jamaican slaves, is a first language for about 10% of the population but is understood by 95%. The population is mostly Muslim (77.1%) with a Christian minority (22.9%), and the largest ethnic groups are Temne, Mende, Limba, and Kono, alongside smaller communities including the Creole, descendants of freed Jamaican slaves settled around Freetown in the late 18th century.
